title: The Town Where Almost All the Children Are Gifted
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler uses Charlottesville's decision to label 86% of students gifted as an entry point to question whether gifted programs deliver anything. A large study found no significant math gains and only a slight reading bump from a year or more of gifted services, and none for Black and most low-income students. She argues that programs cannot advance equity while schools squander most children's potential through weak phonics and skills-based comprehension practice. Tests and teacher judgment favor children with more academic knowledge and vocabulary, which explains underidentification of low-income students. Her proposed alternative is to build academic knowledge for all children from kindergarten rather than rationing enrichment.
points: Relabeling students gifted does not change outcomes; as one board member said, if outcomes are not changing the issue has not been addressed.
A study of about 18,000 elementary students found gifted services associated with no significant math gains and little else, undermining the assumption that the label itself confers advantage.
Gifted programs often focus on projects and critical-thinking activities rather than above-grade content, so they mirror the skills practice that fails in regular classrooms.
Verbal tests and teacher judgment favor children with more academic knowledge and vocabulary, who are disproportionately affluent and highly educated.
Teachers who switched to knowledge-rich curricula report that English learners and special-education students often contribute the most insightful discussion.
quotes: So administrators decided that any student who responded to instruction in regular classrooms and took standardized tests—that is, who didn’t need serious remedial services—would qualify as “gifted.” And voila: the vast majority of Charlottesville students are now “gifted,” with representation of Black and Hispanic students roughly equivalent to their proportions in the school population: 33% are Black, 14% Hispanic, and 42% white.

So it may come as unsettling news to those on both sides that gifted programs, on average, aren’t correlated with increases in test scores. A recent study drawing on data from about 18,000 elementary students across the U.S. found that receiving gifted services for a year or more was associated with no statistically significant gains in math and only a slight bump in reading—and Black and most low-income students didn’t even experience that slight bump. Nor was there any benefit in terms of engagement or motivation.
A large 2019 survey of elementary schools found that most gifted programs focus on projects, games, and activities intended to develop critical thinking and creativity.
But gifted programs will never work as a way to advance equity because our system routinely squanders the potential of huge numbers of children.
The more you know about the topic you’re reading about, the better your comprehension. And the more general academic knowledge you have, the more likely you are to understand whatever you read.

This standard approach may explain why many gifted programs apparently have little effect. If they just provide more “skills” practice but don’t build kids’ substantive knowledge, they’re likely to be just as ineffective as such practice in regular classrooms.

Teachers who have switched to curricula that dive deeply into substantive topics have told me that all their students have blossomed—but especially kids who previously would have been relegated to “low” reading groups. It’s the English-language learners or the children identified as needing special education, they’ve said, who often make the most insightful contributions to class discussion, bringing up concepts and vocabulary introduced months before.
